messages.subject: Detection~Density
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a dataset where density varies an order of magnitude across a ~300,000km2. It is reasonable to assume that animal home ranges vary across this region, and in response to density (food availability).

I know I can add a “costDF” to alter sigma, but I don’t think I can add state-space covariates to the detection model. For my purposes, it might seem inappropriate to have sigma varying, but not detection, as they must be related (sense Efford and Mowat (2014) ‘single-detector sampling area’ a0). Is there any way to get around this? Or, alternatively, is there any reason to think that if I ignore this variation it should produce bias in the D~habitat covariates models?

Cheers,
Clayton

messages.subject: Re: [EXTERNAL] [oscr_package] Detection~Density
messages.body_plain:
Hi!  The costDF will not alter sigma itself, but rather the shape of the detection function on the landscape, which can also be done with an RSF component to your model, e.g., if you have telemetry data.   It should be possible to also incorporate an existing RSF, but I don't think it's standard in oSCR, so you'd probably need to add some code.  The cost DF is most appropriate if you think movement is altered based on habitat, while the RSF component is most appropriate if you think the detection function itself is altered.

If possible, in your case, the RSF component might be the most straightforward.

If you are most interested in D, sigma should be estimated as the mean across your sample (i.e. if you have more with small ranges, will end up more in that direction).

Cheers!

Right now oSCR cannot accommodate spatial variation in sigma, but that could be something worth developing.

Ok this is helpful. Thanks, Tabitha.

I have lots of telemetry data that could be added. I wasn’t certain if it was worth going this route as I already had quite a bit of scr data (~2,000 animals, >4,000 detections) to fit the detection function, and didn’t want to add unnecessary complexity/processing time. But perhaps it is worth it as you suggest.

My real interest is parameterizing structural relationships between population density and habitat covariates. Am I correct that the RSF approach uses telemetry data to fit an RSF to a number of habitat covariates, then uses that RSF in the density model. Is D~RSF and RSF~habitat effectively the same inference as D~habitat (which is what I’m after)?

Yes I have just pooled sigma and p0 across all ranges so far, but I was concerned that overlooking this variability in home range, and detection, could be a a big issue. Do you think it would produce large bias in D~habitat, seeing as home range varies with D?

Cheers,
Clayton

messages.subject: RE: [EXTERNAL] [oscr_package] Detection~Density
messages.body_plain:
Hi Clayton,

The RSF component adjusts the encounter model, it doesn’t directly modulate density.

If you are interested in the density-bearfood relationship, then my sense is that you are going to be okay. A couple of things you could do:

1.      Calculate a trap covariate (on p/g0) which is some function of the food value within a buffer of the trap

2.      You could analyze two subsets of the data (a high density and a low density area, seems like you have the data) and confirm that assuming a single ‘population sigma’ doesn’t have an effect on D.

Chris

Yes I have just pooled sigma and p0 across all ranges so far, but I was concerned that overlooking this variability in home range, and detection, could be a a big issue. Do you think it would produce large bias in D~habitat, seeing as home range varies with D?

Clayton
